FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Compile a differential diagnosis for ulnar-side wrist pain.
Diagnose and manage ulnar impaction and degenerative articular disk tears.
Discuss the surgical indications for ulnar impaction.
Review the outcomes of surgical procedures for the management of ulnar impaction
syndrome.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Ulnar impaction syndrome describes the symptoms produced by contact between the head of
the ulna and the ulnar aspect of the lunate.




NOTES

Repeated contact between the head of the ulna and the lunate may produce changes in the
cartilage and articular disk of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).

Overview
Ulnocarpal impaction (UCI), also known as ulnocarpal abutment, describes the contact
between the ulnar head and the lunate in a wrist with positive ulnar variance. UCI
syndrome is a common source of ulnar-side wrist pain. Associated degenerative changes
occur in the articular disk, and osseous changes occur in the ulnar aspect of the lunate
secondary to contact loading. Some studies suggest that UCI may contribute to
lunotriquetral ligament insufficiency; however, this idea is a subject of debate.
Radiographic signs of UCI may occur in a subset of individuals who have a with positive
ulnar variance, a subset of individuals with impaction have symptoms, a subset of
individuals with symptoms seek specialty care, and a subset of individuals who seek
specialty care request surgical treatment.
Epidemiology
A higher incidence of positive ulnar variance and idiopathic ulnar impaction has been
observed among Asians. The epidemiology of radiographic ulnar impaction and the symptoms
that arise from UCI are unclear. Positive ulnar variance is fairly common but is difficult to
enumerate because of variations in methods of measurement and in the manner in which
radiographs are obtained. Several aspects of the relationship between anatomy,
pathophysiology, and symptoms are uncertain, including the incidence of radiographic
findings consistent with UCI among individuals with positive ulnar variance, the incidence and
timing of symptoms of UCI syndrome among individuals with radiographic findings consistent
with UCI, and the incidence of the pursuit of specialty care among individuals who experience
symptoms from UCI syndrome. Radiographic findings consistent with UCI are common and
often incidental.1 Some studies interpret data regarding positive ulnar variance to indicate a
higher prevalence among Asians than among Caucasians;2-8 however, this interpretation has
not been tested.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The following relative transfer of axial force through the ulna is noted in an experimental
setting:
18% in an ulnar neutral wrist
42% with 2.5 mm of positive ulnar variance
4% with 2.5 mm of negative ulnar variance
The articular disk plays a role in transferring this load from the carpus to the ulna.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Ulnar variance refers to the relative lengths of the distal articular surfaces of the radius
and ulna. By convention, the relative variance is described with reference to the ulna
(ulnar variance); however, the ulna is the fixed object, with the radius changing position
as it pivots over the fixed ulna. A positive ulnar variance increases contact with the
lunate. If this contact is painful, then ulnar impaction syndrome may be diagnosed.1
Ulnar impaction syndrome may occur in a ulnar neutral wrist or a wrist with negative
ulnar variance; however, such occurrences are less common.9
The articular disk absorbs loads between the ulna and the lunate. With greater positive
ulnar variance, the articular disk is thinner, assumes greater load transfer, and may
begin to thin.1
Forearm pronation and grip increase the relative length of the ulna10-12 (Resource 1).
During forearm pronation, dynamic ulnar impaction may occur.13,14 Studies have
demonstrated that ulnar variance changes 1.34 mm during forearm rotation, with ulnar
variance more positive in pronation.4,15
Etiology
UCI and UCI syndrome may occur with positive ulnar variance as a normal variation or after
trauma, including premature physeal arrest of the radius.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
3/23

A large subset of patients can accommodate notable positive ulnar variance after injuries, such
as fracture of the distal radius.

Etiology
Positive ulnar variance may be acquired or congenital, and it is a predisposition for ulnar
impaction. Ulnar impaction may occur after distal radius fracture malunions with relative
shortening of the radius.16,17 A few millimeters of greater positive ulnar variance may
occur over time in patients who undergo radial head excision alone; however, this
variance usually is accommodated. Longitudinal instability of the forearm from rupture
of the interosseous ligament and fracture of the radial head (Essex-Lopresti injury) leads
to marked positive ulnar variance.18,19 Premature physeal arrest of the distal radius in
pediatric patients also may lead to ulnar impaction.20 Finally, ulnar impaction symptoms
may occur in patients who are born with positive ulnar variance.21
Natural History
Ulnar positive variance is related variably to the radiographic signs of UCI.
Radiographic findings of UCI may be accommodated, and radiographic changes frequently are
incidental findings.

Natural History
The natural history of UCI is unknown. Whether the pathology worsens over time
remains unclear. Symptoms of UCI syndrome may have a sudden onset, even if
radiographic imaging studies demonstrate long-standing pathology. The rationale is that
patients may become symptomatic after accumulated degeneration of the TFCC. If a
limited correspondence between the pathology and the symptoms is confirmed, this
rationale requires reconsideration. Long-standing pathology often is misperceived as
new pathology if symptoms begin.22
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
4/23

Risk Factors
Positive ulnar variance may lead to UCI.
Surgeons commonly encounter notable positive ulnar variance during the nonsurgical
management of distal radius fractures. UCI and UCI syndrome seem relatively uncommon.

Risk Factors
Any injury or condition that causes an increase in the length of the ulna relative to the
radius is a predisposing factor for ulnar impaction.1 A cadaver model study by Palmer
and Werner23 reported that wrists with negative ulnar variance had fewer changes in the
lunate cartilage. Ulnar impaction pathology also may occur in wrists with relatively
neutral ulnar variance because the ulna is relatively positive during forearm pronation
and gripping. How often ulnar impaction pathology occurs in wrists with neutral ulnar
variance, how often ulnar impaction causes symptoms, or how ulnar impaction can be
diagnosed reliably and accurately remain unclear.13,14
Classification
Degeneration of the articular disk may result from impact between the ulnar head and the
lunate.
No classification system exists that is based on variations in the severity of cartilage and
articular disk degeneration.

Classification
Palmer24 classified degenerative pathology of the articular disk according to the
presence or absence of associated lesions diagnosed during wrist arthroscopy. The
ability to distinguish UCI pathology from the natural degeneration of the articular disk
(present in nearly two-thirds of adults aged 50 to 69 years) is, to the knowledge of the
authors of this lesson, untested.25

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
UCI syndrome is characterized by ulnar-side wrist pain.
Pain may be noted on ulnar deviation during power gripping, especially if combined with
rotation of the forearm.

Patient History
Ulnar impaction is characterized by ulnar wrist pain generally and by ulnar deviation
particularly. A progressive and insidious onset of symptoms may occur or the symptoms
may be noticed suddenly, sometimes after a specific event, in which the impaction may
feel similar to an injury. Pain may be noted during forearm rotation because of changes
in the dynamic length of the ulna.13,14
Physical Examination
A positive ulnocarpal stress test (pain during manipulation of the wrist into ulnar deviation and
rotation of the forearm) supports the diagnosis of UCI syndrome.
Because a positive ulnocarpal stress test may occur with other pathologies, the diagnosis of
UCI syndrome is made if the symptoms and the physical examination correspond with
radiographic pathology.

Physical Examination
Examples of pathologies that may cause pain on the ulnar side of the wrist include distal
radioulnar joint (DRUJ) laxity, DRUJ arthritis, extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) tendinitis with
or without subluxation, lunotriquetral ligament insufficiency, pisotriquetral arthritis, and
neuritis of the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve. These pathologies are
anatomically distinct and—with the exception of lunotriquetral pathology, which is
uncommon and quite variably diagnosed—should be straightforward to discern.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
6/23

Reproduction of pain during the ulnocarpal compression test, which involves placing the
wrist in ulnar deviation, axially loading the carpus into the ulna, and passively rotating
the forearm, is sensitive for the diagnosis of UCI syndrome.26 This maneuver also can
cause pain in patients with articular disk and distal radioulnar ligament pathology,
lunotriquetral pathology, or arthritis. Foveal tenderness can be evaluated for avulsion of
the DRUJ ligament origin or ulnar extrinsic ligament tears; however, this may be difficult
to discern and is less likely to occur in combination with radiographic UCI.
Lunotriquetral ligament pathology can be evaluated via the shuck and compression
tests. The shuck test, also known as the ballottement test, is performed by grasping the
lunate between the thumb and index finger of one hand and applying dorsal and palmar
load while stabilizing the triquetrum with the thumb and index finger of the other hand.
Pain, crepitus, or increased laxity is indicative of a positive test. The lunotriquetral
compression test involves manually compressing the triquetrum into the lunate. A
positive test results in pain or crepitus. The reliability and diagnostic performance of
these tests has been questioned.
Neurovascular Examination
The ulnar nerve and artery should be examined for signs of compression or thrombosis as
potential causes of symptoms on the ulnar side of the wrist.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs can be used to confirm UCI syndrome suspected based on the patient history and
physical examination.
A PA radiograph of the wrist in neutral rotation is used to measure ulnar variance.
Radiographic measurements may help discern the degree to which UCI results from radius
deformity (eg, mild Madelung disease or prior distal radius deformity).
Radiographic comparison with the contralateral wrist may help discern pathology from
variation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
7/23


Radiography
If the patient history and physical examination suggest a specific pathology to a
reasonable probability, radiographs may be useful. The probability of a correct diagnosis
increases if the symptoms and signs correspond with discrete pathology observed on
radiographs.
A PA and grip view (obtained with the wrist in neutral rotation and the elbow at 90°),
oblique view, and lateral view may help determine the maximum ulnar variance and aid
in evaluation for radiographic evidence of UCI, such as changes in the subchondral bone
of the ulnar head or the ulnar corner of the lunate. Ulnar variance is measured as the
distance between two lines perpendicular to the longitudinal axis of the radius, one line
tangential to the distal point of the ulnar head and the other line tangential to the distal
articular surface of the lunate fossa. Variation in the measurement of ulnar variance may
occur if measurement is begun from the volar margin of the lunate facet, which typically
is more distinct, rather than taking care to measure from a point midway between the
volar and dorsal margins of the articular surface, which accounts for any variance in
radial angulation or angulation in the projection of the radiograph. Deformity of the
radius may contribute to positive ulnar variance via distal radius fracture malunion,
premature physeal arrest, or mild Madelung deformity. Lateral radiographs can be
evaluated for dorsal ulnar subluxation and—if subluxation is a potential cause of
symptoms—subluxation can be confirmed via CT in various positions of forearm
rotation. Contralateral radiographs also should be reviewed because patients may have
accommodated ulnar positive variance in both upper extremities.
Computed Tomography
Although CT arthrography allows for assessment of the ligaments of the wrist with high
sensitivity and specificity for pathology (wrist arthroscopy as the reference standard), its use is
limited compared with MRI.27,28
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
8/23

MRI is best used selectively to confirm expected pathology in patients in whom surgical
treatment is being considered.
MRI shows many normal variations and accommodated changes; therefore, MRI may be
misleading and unhelpful in a scenario of low pretest probability (eg, nonspecific wrist pain).
If the likelihood of UCI is high based on the symptoms, physical examination findings, and
radiographic findings, but the radiographic findings are not specific for UCI, MRI can confirm or
exclude the diagnosis of UCI to determine if surgical management may be helpful.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
UCI syndrome is diagnosed based on patient history and physical examination findings,
with the potential for UCI to be confirmed on radiographs. MRI has limited utility. MRI
may be helpful in the uncommon setting in which UCI may be the cause of UCI syndrome
but radiographic findings are not definitive. Using MRI indiscriminately (eg, for
unexplained pain) creates a notable potential for harmful overinterpretation of
incidental findings, including incidental signs of UCI. In patients with characteristic
symptoms and signs of ulnar impaction syndrome, MRI may help detect subtle findings,
such as chondromalacia and bone marrow edema. Kienböck disease typically is
observed as total or subtotal lunate changes on MRI, whereas lesions from ulnar
impaction generally are localized to the proximal ulnar aspect of the lunate.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography plays no role in the diagnosis of ulnar impaction.
Ultrasonography plays no role in the diagnosis of ulnar impaction; however, in patients in
whom ECU tendinitis or instability is included in the differential diagnosis, ultrasonography
may be particularly useful for providing a dynamic assessment of the ECU tendon. In addition,
ultrasonography can be used to evaluate for masses, fluid collections, foreign bodies,
compression peripheral neuropathy, or abnormal blood flow.29,30
Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
9/23

Despite a thoughtful patient history and physical examination with or without radiographs, a
large percentage of wrist pain is never associated with a specific pathophysiology. The clinician
and the patient must be comfortable with this inherent uncertainty.
The diagnosis of UCI syndrome is based on specific symptoms; discrete reproducible signs;
and supportive imaging studies, which is almost always limited to radiographs alone. If doubt
exists with regard to the correspondence of symptoms with radiographic findings, then
caution is warranted, nonspecific diagnoses are favored, and the diagnosis of UCI should be
withheld.
Differential Diagnosis
Most of the other causes of nontraumatic pain on the ulnar side of the wrist are discrete and
can be discerned from UCI syndrome. A few causes that are less discrete, difficult to discern,
and variably diagnosed from surgeon to surgeon are more open to debate.
Osseous
Kienböck disease (global wrist pain, limited passive motion)
DRUJ arthritis (pain and crepitus on forearm rotation or translation on compression)
Pisotriquetral arthritis (discrete pain directly over the pisiform, confirmed via CT)
Suggested entities that are difficult to discern, with wide surgeon-to-surgeon variation in
diagnosis include a hamate arthrosis lunotriquetral ligament tear with type II lunates, which
is open to debate and typically diagnosed via diagnostic wrist arthroscopy, the utility of which
can be questioned
Ligamentous
Articular disk pathology unrelated to UCI—These pathologies should be implicated with
caution because the causes of pain as signal are eventually present in two-thirds of
individuals. If a high base rate of inferably accommodated changes exist, accurately
association of such changes with symptoms is difficult.
DRUJ laxity—In the absence of asymmetric subluxation or dislocation, this condition is
difficult to define and measure. This is a variable and inconsistent diagnosis and should be
considered with caution.
Suggested entities that are difficult to discern, with wide surgeon-to-surgeon variation in
diagnosis include:
Lunotriquetral ligament pathology
Ulnotriquetral ligament pathology
Tendinous—Discretely tender and provocable
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
10/23

ECU tendinopathy
ECU laxity
Extensor digiti minimi tendinopathy (rare)
Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) tendinopathy (rare)
Neurologic—Discrete and provocable
Ulnar neuropathy at the Guyon canal
Dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar neuropathy
Vascular—Ulnar artery thrombosis (diagnosed via the Allen test)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Patient counseling—Patients should understand why the wrist hurts and that arm use is safe
even if uncomfortable.
Nonspecific palliative measures (nonopioid analgesic agents, ice or heat, splints)
Time for potential accommodation (Resource 2)

Nonsurgical Management
Symptoms generally are self-limiting. A splint may limit symptoms. Patients may choose
to avoid some painful activities, but it is safe to continue with valued painful activities in
the context of UCI. Acetaminophen and NSAIDs may be helpful. The role of steroid
injection is less clear. Patients who are not satisfied with these measures and have
discrete pathology can be offered surgical treatment. Roh et al31 reported that surgical
treatment failure was associated with female sex,31 longer symptom duration, and more
intense pain on initial presentation.
Surgical Management
Patients diagnosed with UCI who are not satisfied with accommodation and palliation can be
offered an ulnar-shortening osteotomy (USO) or the wafer procedure in combination with
wrist arthroscopy.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
11/23

A USO allows for more shortening than the wafer procedure.
Indications

Indications
History, physical examination findings, and radiographic evidence of ulnar impaction in a
patient dissatisfied with accommodation and palliative treatment. An USO may be the
only treatment option if more than 3 mm of shortening is necessary.
Contraindications
Contraindications to USO include DRUJ dislocation and DRUJ arthritis.
Smoking is a relative contraindication because it delays union time and decreases union rates.

Contraindications
DRUJ arthritis and instability are contraindications for ulnar shortening procedures
because symptoms may worsen. Because USO corrects only the relationship of the ulna
to the carpus, radiocarpal malalignment from distal radius malunion is not addressed.
Finally, any local soft-tissue infection should be eradicated before proceeding with USO.
Smoking may be considered a relative contraindication for USO because it has been
associated with an increased potential for nonunion in some case series.
Techniques/Procedures
Ulnar Shortening Osteotomy

Ulnar Shortening Osteotomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
12/23

The authors of this lesson prefer the surgical technique described by Chun and Palmer32
(Resource 3). Wrist arthroscopy can be performed at the time of USO for diagnostic
purposes or for débridement of the TFCC.
Preoperative Planning

Preoperative Planning
Preoperatively, standard PA radiographs in neutral forearm rotation and pronated grip
radiographs are obtained and compared with those of the contralateral wrist. The goal is
to shorten the ulna to a slightly negative ulnar variance.33
Patient Positioning

Patient Positioning
For USO, the patient is placed in the supine position with the surgical extremity on a
radiolucent hand table. A nonsterile arm tourniquet is used for hemostasis.
If wrist arthroscopy is performed at the time of USO, then the shoulder is placed in
abduction and the elbow is flexed to 90°. The arm is secured to the table with the use of
a Velcro strap or a soft wrap. Traction is then applied through finger traps to distract the
wrist. The arthroscopy setup can be maintained or taken down before USO. The
arthroscopy setup may facilitate surgery and positioning for ulnar side dissection and
shortening. This setup may be particularly helpful if the surgeon is performing the
procedure with minimal assistance.
Surgical Approaches

Surgical Approaches
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
13/23

The surgical interval lies between the ECU and the FCU. The skin is incised along the
subcutaneous boarder of the ulna approximately 10 cm proximal from the ulnar neck.
The fascia is then incised between the ECU and FCU. The dorsal sensory branches of the
ulnar nerve lie volar and distal to the exposure; therefore, they should be carefully
protected during exposure. The length of the incision should be adequate to
accommodate a 6-hole or 7-hole, 3.5-mm plate. The muscle is elevated, and the
periosteum is left in place to optimize biologic aspects of healing.
Osteotomy and Fixation

Osteotomy and Fixation
Ulnar osteotomy can be performed with the use of implant systems that provide the
implant and the cutting jig; alternatively, it can be performed free hand with parallel
cuts.
Two oblique cuts are marked through the center of the plate. A longitudinal mark is
created to preserve rotation of the ulna. At 45° to the coronal plane, an incomplete
oblique cut is made through the ulna, approximately 75%. A second cut is made parallel
to the first cut to allow for the desired amount of shortening. The kerf of the saw blade
should be accounted for when making the second cut. A 6-hole or 7-hole, 3.5-mm plate
is used to secure the ulna. Axial compression is applied manually, and the plate is
clamped and fixed to the ulna. One or two of the proximal screws are inserted
eccentrically to compress the osteotomy.
Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
For comfort, the authors of this lesson prefer to immobilize the wrist in an ulnar gutter
splint for 2 weeks postoperatively; however, this is optional. Hand and forearm motion
and stretching are encouraged. After 2 weeks postoperatively, the patient is transitioned
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
14/23

to a removable splint, and wrist motion and stretches are encouraged. Strenuous activity
and lifting are restricted until union is observed on radiographs.
Metaphyseal Osteotomy
The ulna also can be shortened via a closing wedge metaphyseal osteotomy, leaving
the ulnar periosteum intact and fixed with the use of a single buried headless screw.34
A distal osteotomy through metaphyseal bone may heal more reliably than a
diaphyseal osteotomy.
Tilting the ulnar head may alter the DRUJ articulation; whether this has any effect
remains unclear.
Wafer Procedure
In this procedure, 2 to 4 mm of the ulnar head is excised.35 The procedure originally was
described as an open procedure; however, it currently is commonly performed
arthroscopically.
Preoperative Planning

Preoperative Planning
Preoperatively, standard PA radiographs in neutral forearm rotation and pronated grip
radiographs are obtained and compared with those of the contralateral wrist. The goal is
to resect enough of the ulnar head to create negative ulnar variance without resecting
more than 4 mm.
Patient Positioning
Open—The patient is positioned supine with the surgical extremity on a radiolucent hand
table. A nonsterile arm tourniquet is used for hemostasis.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
15/23

Arthroscopic—The patient is positioned supine with the surgical extremity on a radiolucent
hand table. A nonsterile arm tourniquet is used for hemostasis. The shoulder is abducted, and
the elbow is flexed to 90°. The arm is secured to the table using a Velcro strap or a soft wrap.
Traction is then applied through finger traps to distract the wrist.
Surgical Approaches
Open—A dorsal approach over the DRUJ is used. A 5-cm incision is made between the fifth and
sixth extensor compartments. Care is taken to protect and preserve the dorsal ulnar sensory
branches. The extensor compartment of the extensor digitorum quinti is released, and the
extensor digitorum quinti is retracted. An L-shaped or U-shaped capsulotomy is made to
access the ulnar head and the TFCC. The dome of the ulnar head is resected 3 to 4 mm with
the use of an osteotome or oscillating saw, with careful attention paid to preserving the TFCC.
Arthroscopic—The 3-4 portal is used as a viewing portal for the arthroscope, and a burr is
placed into the 6-R portal. The ulnar head is then resected 3 to 4 mm through the defect in the
articular disk. If the defect in the articular disk is not large enough, then a distal radioulnar
joint portal can be established beneath the TFCC to perform the resection.
Postoperative Management

Postoperative Management
The patient’s arm is immobilized in a sugar tong splint for comfort for 2 weeks
postoperatively, after which the patient is transitioned to a removable Velcro wrist splint.
Strenuous activity and lifting are not recommended for as many as 8 to 12 weeks
postoperatively.
Complications
Nonunion
The rate of nonunion after USO is approximately 5%.
The wafer procedure avoids the risk of nonunion but alters the DRUJ joint.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
16/23


Nonunion
One of the more common complications of USO is nonunion. The nonunion rate from
USO is approximately 5%36,37 (Resource 4). Minimal elevation of muscle and periosteum
may limit disruption of the blood supply to the ulna. In addition, copious irrigation
during the osteotomy may help limit thermal injury to the bone. Some studies suggest
that transverse osteotomies are more prone to nonunion than oblique osteotomies.38
An osteotomy at the metaphysis improves metaphyseal bone healing. Smoking increases
the risk of USO nonunion or delayed union.39
Persistent Pain
Patients with persistent postoperative pain can be evaluated for technical and mechanical
etiologies, such as persistent UCI, irritation from the plate and screws, or nonunion.
Infection
Postoperative infection can occur after a USO or wafer procedure.
The management of postoperative infection may consist of oral antibiotic agents for the
management of a superficial infection or débridement and intravenous antibiotic agents for
the management of a deep infection.

Infection
Postoperative infection after USO can be managed via débridement and antibiotic
agents until healing given that the plate is not loose.40 If the osteotomy is solidly healed
at a minimum of 12 months postoperatively, then the plate can be removed or
suppressive antibiotic agents can be stopped. Surgical treatment can be performed in
patients in whom infection recurs.
Hardware Irritation
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
17/23

Plate placement can be dorsal, volar, or directly ulnar.
Debate exists regarding which position is better for plate prominence and tendon
irritation.41,42
If patients request implant removal, surgeons should wait at least 12 to 18 months
postoperatively to decrease the risk of refracture.33
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The dorsal sensory nerve can be anticipated in the distal part of the dissection if the incision is
near the wrist.

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The dorsal ulnar sensory nerve passes from volar to dorsal at the level of the ulnar head.
During direct ulnar exposure of the interval between the FCU and the ECU, the nerve
should be protected with blunt dissection in the distal part of the wound near the wrist.
Outcomes
Case series report improved symptoms in most patients after USO and wafer procedures.
Limited comparative data found no differences between the two procedures.
No comparisons with simulated surgery controls account for nonspecific effects; improvement
is unrelated to alteration in pathology.
The relative advantages and disadvantages of the wafer procedure and various techniques for
USO are subjects of debate.

Outcomes
Case series of USO and wafer procedures report improvement of symptoms in most
patients. The results of USO and the wafer procedure are similar.43 Patients who
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:58 AM
AAOS | Ulnar Impaction
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000025
18/23

undergo USO may have hardware irritation or nonunion. Patients who undergo the
wafer procedure are at risk for stylocarpal abutment from a prominent ulnar styloid.
